Design Quarterly 133:
“Does It Make Sense?”

April Greiman’s issue of the Walker Art Center’s journal, made on a Macintosh as a single fold-out poster: a life-size bitmap self-portrait among layers of type, symbols, and video images.

Source
People’s Graphic Design Archive: Design Quarterly #133
Creator
April Greiman
Made
1986 (Walker Art Center)
Styles
New Wave typography (partial fit; agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person), Pixel Art (partial fit; agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Layered, experimental, intuitive, digital
Evidence
Inspected the People’s Graphic Design Archive photographs of the front and back of one opened copy (1440 × 474 and 1440 × 485) in scratchpad copies. The owner of the copy is not stated. Only the larger type is readable at this size. Not stored.

28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Walker Art Center text quoted by the People’s Graphic Design Archive says the usual 32 pages were treated as a two-foot-by-six-foot, double-sided fold-out, and that Greiman used MacDraw to combine video images and type and to tile pages into a pixelated, life-size double self-portrait. People’s Graphic Design Archive.

Greiman’s own page names Mildred Friedman as editor and says the type was set on a Macintosh and LaserWriter. aprilgreiman.com.

Observed

  • The front is dark violet on cream. A life-size nude figure made of coarse bitmap dots lies across the whole sheet.
  • Around the figure float a spiral galaxy, hands, a brain, orbits, planet symbols, small photographs, and a black panel with a moon.
  • A bitmap block at the top right holds large pixel numerals and “the spiritual double” in a monospaced face.
  • A line of words runs along the bottom edge on a ruled scale: “proton . neutron . electron . moron . milli . micro …”, with wide gaps and full stops between the words.
  • “live where you can.” sits upside down on a white bar.
  • The back has large colour video stills, a yellow ground, a dot-screen cloud in orange, blue text in a slab face, and narrow columns of small text.

Why it belongs

The issue keeps the style’s layering, bars, and spaced lines, but the type is often monospaced or slab, and bitmap dots replace film screens. It is a partial fit that marks the end of the period and the start of digital postmodern design.

The monospaced lines here are one reason the fingerprint should not treat a small share of monospaced type as a counter-sign by itself.

Borrow

Run a spaced-out line of words along a ruled scale at the page edge.

Build one large figure from coarse dots and lay small symbols over it.

Turn one short phrase upside down on a white bar.
